questions.q: What is the primary difference between a packet-filtering firewall and a stateful inspection firewall in terms of connection tracking?
questions.a: A packet-filtering firewall examines each packet in isolation (source/destination IP, port, protocol) without remembering past packets, while a stateful inspection firewall maintains a state table tracking active connections (e.g., TCP handshake stages) and allows return traffic only for initiated sessions. A wrong answer (e.g., "both track connections") reveals the student confuses stateless ACLs with dynamic stateful logic, a common error when they memorize definitions without understanding the TCP state machine.

questions.q: A student configures their host firewall to "Allow all outbound traffic" and "Block all inbound traffic except established/related." They claim this makes their laptop completely safe from malware downloads. Explain why this reasoning is flawed.
questions.a: The rule allows the student to initiate a connection to a malicious website (outbound allowed), download malware (return traffic is "established"), and execute it. The firewall only filters network traffic, not file content. A wrong answer (e.g., "inbound block stops downloads") shows the student misunderstands that "established" return packets carry the malicious payload, and that firewalls do not inspect application-layer content like antivirus does.

questions.q:
You are given a firewall log snippet: 
```
TIMESTAMP       SRC_IP        DST_IP        PROTO  SPORT  DPORT  ACTION
10:00:01        203.0.113.5   192.168.1.10  TCP    54321  22     ALLOW
10:00:02        203.0.113.5   192.168.1.10  TCP    54321  22     ALLOW
10:00:03        203.0.113.5   192.168.1.10  TCP    54321  3389   DENY
10:00:04        203.0.113.5   192.168.1.10  TCP    54322  445    DENY
```
Identify the likely attack pattern and state which firewall rule (from a default-deny policy) would have explicitly allowed the first two lines.
questions.a: The log shows port scanning (SSH on 22 succeeded, then RDP 3389 and SMB 445 probed). The first two lines were allowed by a rule: "ALLOW TCP FROM ANY TO 192.168.1.10 PORT 22" (SSH access). A wrong answer (e.g., "allow all from 203.0.113.5") indicates inability to read logs and infer the minimal necessary rule, a critical skill for board exam log-analysis questions.

questions.q: Compare signature-based and heuristic-based antivirus detection in terms of: (a) ability to detect zero-day malware, (b) false positive rate, (c) resource consumption during scan. Present as a table.
questions.a:
| Aspect                | Signature-based                     | Heuristic-based                         |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Zero-day detection    | Poor (needs prior sample)           | Good (behavioral patterns)              |
| False positive rate   | Very low (exact match)              | Moderate to high (suspicious behavior)  |
| Resource consumption  | Low (hash/lookup)                   | Higher (emulation/code analysis)        |
A wrong answer swapping false positive rates shows the student memorized definitions but not the operational trade-offs examiners test in "justify your choice" questions.

questions.q: Your school lab has 50 PCs. The IT admin installs a free antivirus that updates signatures once a week via manual USB. Evaluate this strategy against the criteria of "timeliness," "consistency," and "attack surface." Recommend a better approach with justification.
questions.a: Evaluation: Timeliness – poor (weekly gap allows new malware); Consistency – low (manual process fails if admin absent); Attack surface – high (USB itself can spread malware). Better approach: Deploy a centrally managed antivirus with automatic hourly cloud updates over the LAN, using a local update mirror to save bandwidth. This ensures timeliness (hourly), consistency (automated), and reduces attack surface (no USB). A wrong answer suggesting "daily manual updates" fails to address consistency and USB risk, missing the enterprise-management concept.

questions.q: Design a minimal firewall rule set (max 5 rules) for a home router protecting a LAN (192.168.1.0/24) that hosts a web server (192.168.1.50) accessible from the internet on port 80/443, allows all outbound web browsing, and blocks everything else. Write rules in order with ACTION, PROTOCOL, SOURCE, DESTINATION, PORT.
questions.a:
1. ALLOW TCP ANY 192.168.1.50 80,443 (inbound web)
2. ALLOW TCP 192.168.1.0/24 ANY 80,443 (outbound web)
3. ALLOW UDP 192.168.1.0/24 ANY 53 (DNS for browsing)
4. ALLOW ICMP ANY ANY (ping/traceroute for diagnostics)
5. DENY ANY ANY ANY ANY (implicit default, but explicit for clarity)
A poor answer includes "ALLOW ANY ANY ANY" or misses DNS, showing inability to apply least-privilege principle and understand dependency protocols.
